column3: Exact parallel: it asks whether someone has taken a covenant with the Most Merciful, the stated condition in the focus ayah.
Divine dominion over forgiveness and punishment supports the focus ayah's denial of independently held intercessory power.
It rejects proposed intercessors that possess nothing, directly clarifying why intercession cannot be independently owned.
It likewise denies intercessory power except to those who testify to truth knowingly, supplying a qualifying condition.
Idris being raised to a high station does not clarify covenant-conditioned intercession.
Seeking honor from a source other than God broadly parallels locating an authority where it is not possessed.
It explicitly limits useful intercession to one authorized by the Most Merciful and whose speech He accepts.
Blessing upon the Prophet concerns a different directed relation, not intercession or covenant.
Fulfilling a covenant and fearing God gives a general ethical frame for the covenant named in the focus ayah.
Permission from the Most Merciful to speak on the Last Day parallels the focus ayah's restricted authorization.
The preceding gathering of the righteous to the Most Merciful supplies the immediate eschatological setting for the focus ayah.
It rejects the idolaters' unsupported claim that their objects are intercessors with God.
It states that intercession avails only for one whom God permits, matching the focus ayah's limitation.
Faithful fulfillment of a pledge offers only a general covenant parallel, without intercession.
The judgment of angel worshippers is relevant only as background to false intermediary claims.
No creature possesses independent right of address before the Most Merciful, reinforcing restricted standing.
Mary's provision at the palm tree is unrelated to intercession or covenant.
Its rejection of an unproven rival deity broadly supports exclusive divine authority but not the focus rule itself.
It assigns all intercession to God, directly grounding the focus ayah's denial of independent possession.
The identification of Jesus in the Mary narrative does not clarify intercession or covenant.
Even angels' intercession is ineffective until God permits and approves it, closely matching the focus limitation.
The claim that the Most Merciful has taken a child begins the immediate passage's rejection of improper divine relations.
Keeping a pledge to God is a general covenant parallel without an intercessory role.
God's dominion provides broad authority background but adds no specific condition on intercession.
It rejects calling honored servants children of the Most Merciful, a nearby theological boundary on divine relations.
The annunciation to Mary is unrelated to covenant-conditioned intercession.
The condemned people's lack of intercessors illustrates the absence of any available advocacy, though not its condition.
Powerless fabricated deities cannot control benefit or harm, supporting the denial of independent intermediary power.
The destruction of earlier generations does not clarify intercession or covenant.
The oath by the even and odd is not an intercession reference.
It denies provision to false objects and directs seeking to God, a broad exclusive-authority parallel.
Breaking God's covenant shows its binding seriousness, though the ayah does not address intercession.
Its treaty covenant concerns human political obligations rather than standing with the Most Merciful.
It challenges an unsupported claim to have taken a covenant with God, closely paralleling the focus ayah's covenant criterion.
Mary's labor scene does not clarify intercession or covenant.
Exclusive knowledge of the unseen only broadly supports God's control over eschatological matters.
It denies that alleged associates possess anything or assist God, directly supporting the exclusion of autonomous intercessors.
No one can control benefit or harm against God, broadly reinforcing exclusive divine authority.
Satan's claim to take an allotted share does not clarify authorized intercession.
It rejects the unsupported assertion that God has taken a child, continuing the theological boundary relevant to the passage.
The gathering around Hell is only general Last-Day context for the focus ayah.
Its account of hypocrites' reactions to gain and loss is unrelated.
Discarding covenants illustrates covenant failure but does not illuminate intercessory standing.
Fulfilling God's covenant establishes its binding character, though not the focus ayah's authorization rule.
The alternatives of victory or punishment do not clarify intercession or covenant.
It warns against trading God's covenant for little gain, a broad covenant parallel only.
Moses' description as messenger and prophet does not clarify the focus ayah.
Taking God as guardian broadly directs reliance to the sole authority, without discussing intercession.
Its warning against claiming that God has taken a child supports the same theological boundary as the surrounding passage.
It shows that intercessors' intercession does not avail the condemned, a direct negative boundary for the focus theme.
Invalid worship at the House does not clarify covenant-conditioned intercession.
Protection from a second death does not bear on intercession or covenant.
Ishmael's truthfulness in promise is only a broad pledge-related parallel.
God's knowledge of hostile schemes does not clarify the focus rule.
Security from God's plan is unrelated to intercession or covenant.
Denying the Day of Judgment gives only broad judgment context for intercession.
The calf cannot answer or control harm or benefit, reinforcing the incapacity of false objects to mediate.
Turning away from a reminder of the Most Merciful does not clarify intercession.
Abraham's critique of an unhearing, unseeing object broadly parallels the incapacity of false mediators.
Mocking divine signs is unrelated to covenant-conditioned intercession.
It explicitly says false gods' intercession would not benefit or rescue one from the Most Merciful's harm.
The garden near the lote tree does not clarify intercession or covenant.
The truth-bound descent of angels is unrelated to the focus ayah.
God's displeasure at saying what one does not do is only a distant truthfulness parallel to covenant.
Naming God the Most Merciful establishes a general divine identity but adds no intercession condition.
Regret over taking a friend does not clarify authorized intercession.
All beings come to the Most Merciful as servants, reinforcing that no creature has independent standing before Him.
The appeal to Moses by a covenant with him only faintly parallels an authorized relational appeal.
The divine name alone adds no specific intercession relation.
A conditional vow to God is a general covenant instance, not a criterion for intercession.
Revelation from the Most Merciful does not clarify intercession or covenant.
God's different measure of time does not clarify the focus ayah.
The divine names alone do not establish a neighbor relation.
A favor from God does not address intercession or covenant.
Treating expenditure as a means of nearness to God gives a broad relation-to-God parallel, not intercession.
Taking the calf after clear signs broadly resembles misplaced religious attachment, without intercession.
The idolaters' fatalistic claim about the Most Merciful does not clarify the focus rule.
The summary of disliked acts before God is unrelated to intercession or covenant.
It denies any army can aid people apart from the Most Merciful, broadly reinforcing exclusive divine help.
It says the alleged partners will not be intercessors, directly rejecting false intermediary expectations.
The divine names and knowledge of seen and unseen do not specify intercession.
Taking the calf is a distant example of false attachment rather than authorized intercession.
It denies that chosen protectors possess benefit or harm, reinforcing the exclusion of independent mediating power.
Accountability for a covenant supplies only a general covenant parallel.
The deniers' claim that the Most Merciful sent nothing does not clarify intercession.

The exclusive religion with God does not clarify intercession or covenant.
God's covenant not reaching wrongdoers gives a general limitation on covenantal status.
Calling idols enemies except for the Lord of the worlds does not address intercession.
Abraham cannot control anything for his father against God, a broad limit on personal advocacy.
Deliverance from distress does not clarify intercession or covenant.
No person can control benefit or harm for another on that Day, supporting the focus ayah's denial of autonomous power.
The superiority of God's judgment does not specifically concern intercession.
Reward and mutual approval before God faintly echo a qualified relation to Him, without intercession.
Emergence from graves is general eschatological context only.
A request for a home near God is a spatial-nearness parallel, not covenantal intercession.
False invoked beings cannot remove harm or withhold mercy, broadly excluding independent rival powers.
Taking false gods in hope of help illustrates misplaced reliance on beings unable to provide saving support.
It states the governing rule directly: none can intercede with God except by His permission.
Its Last-Day warning that there is no intercession establishes the default exclusion that the focus ayah qualifies.
It treats intercession as an act with accountable consequences, though it does not state the divine authorization condition.
It warns of meeting God with no protector or intercessor besides Him, directly denying alternative advocacy.
At judgment, the claimed intercessors are absent, exposing unsupported reliance on them.
The condemned ask whether any intercessors can intercede for them, illustrating the irreversible loss of advocacy.
It expressly says there is no intercessor except after His permission, closely paralleling the focus ayah.
Those invoked besides God cannot remove or transfer harm, supporting the incapacity of rival mediators.
The honored servants do not intercede except for one God approves, supplying an explicit approval condition.
It states that none besides God can be protector or intercessor, reinforcing exclusive divine control of advocacy.
The false gods are worshipped as a supposed means of nearness to God, clarifying the error behind unauthorized mediation.
On the approaching Day, there is no intimate friend or intercessor whose plea is obeyed, a direct limiting counterpart.
The throne-bearing angels seek forgiveness for believers, a concrete but non-identical form of divinely situated advocacy.
The alleged gods taken as means of nearness fail their worshippers, reinforcing the collapse of false mediation.
